title: A deep read of T5: every task as text in, text out, then change one variable at a time
summary: T5 turns translation, classification, summarization, and even scoring into “text in, text out,” then starts from one baseline and systematically compares architecture, pretraining objective, data, fine-tuning approach, and scale. We do the arithmetic on why span corruption saves compute, walk through each controlled comparison, and flag a duplicated table row.
ai_summary: “Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer” (Raffel et al., Google, JMLR 2020) casts all NLP tasks into a text-to-text format, then compares architecture, pretraining objective, dataset, fine-tuning and multitask strategy, and scaling on a roughly 220-million-parameter encoder-decoder baseline. It also releases C4, about 750GB of cleaned web text. Conclusions: an encoder-decoder with a denoising objective performs best; denoising variants are similar, so choose by compute cost; too much data repetition is harmful; increasing model size usually beats training longer. The largest T5, 11B parameters, was state of the art on 18 of 24 tasks at the time.
brief: The problem: pretraining recipes were multiplying, with objective, data, architecture, and scale all changing at once — making it hard to tell which choices actually matter.
The method: cast every task into text-to-text format, start from one baseline and change a single factor at a time, and clean the C4 corpus.
Results: encoder-decoder plus span-corruption denoising wins; data should be large and clean; a bigger model usually beats more training; T5-11B achieves state of the art on 18 tasks.
Limitations: changing one factor at a time can miss interactions; translation never beat the prior best; Table 10 has a row that looks like a copy-paste error.

paper.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
paper.authors: Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, Peter J. Liu

cover.headline: A close reading of the T5 paper
cover.highlight: Everything is text in, text out

sections.h: First, the bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In October 2019, nine Google researchers — Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, and others — released this 67-page paper; it was published in 2020 in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR). The model it introduces is **T5**, short for Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer.

Its motivation is pragmatic: after BERT and GPT in 2018, pretraining methods exploded. Every paper changed the objective, the data, the architecture, or the scale, making it hard to tell which change actually helped. The paper says its main goal is **not to propose a new method**; it is to compare existing approaches systematically in a single unified framework.

The unified framework is **text-to-text**: translation, summarization, QA, classification, and even regression-style scoring are all written as “text in, text out.” For translation, the input is “translate English to German: That is good.” and the output is “Das ist gut.” To judge whether a sentence is grammatical, output “acceptable” or “not acceptable.” That allows every task to use **one model, one loss function, one set of hyperparameters, and one decoding process.**

Within this framework, the paper starts from a single baseline and changes one factor at a time: architecture, pretraining objective, pretraining data, fine-tuning approach, multitask training, and scaling. To support that, it also cleans a roughly 750GB corpus of English web text called **C4**. Finally it combines the best choices, trains a model with up to 11 billion parameters, and achieves state of the art on 18 of 24 tasks at that time.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Turn every NLP task into “text in, text out,” then run it like a controlled experiment: change one variable at a time and systematically answer “which pretraining choices actually matter.” The answer: encoder-decoder + span corruption + large, clean data + a bigger model.

callout.title: Three concepts you need before reading
callout.text: If you’re not familiar with them, these are the essentials:
list: **Pretraining + fine-tuning**: train on massive unlabeled text first, then continue training on a small amount of labeled data for the specific task. See the GPT-1 and BERT deep reads.
**Encoder-decoder**: the encoder reads the input, the decoder writes the output one token at a time, and attention connects them. See the Transformer deep read.
**Masked language model**: mask some input tokens and make the model guess them. This is the objective BERT uses.

sections.h: Text-to-text: one format for every task

blocks.p: The paper’s approach: prepend a **task prefix** to the original input to tell the model what to do, and the output is simply the answer as text.

fig.title: How different tasks become “text in, text out”
fig.subtitle: Examples from Figure 1 and Section 2.4 of the paper
rows: translate English to German: That is good.
cola sentence: The course is jumping well.
stsb sentence1: The rhino grazed on the grass. sentence2: A rhino is grazing in a field.
mnli premise: I hate pigeons. hypothesis: My feelings towards pigeons are filled with animosity.
summarize: state authorities dispatched emergency crews tuesday to survey the damage…
six people hospitalized after a storm in attala county.

plain.title: Every task is “text in, text out”
plain.text: Translation, summarization, acceptability judgment, and the rest used to need their own output heads. T5 adds a task name before the input (`translate:`, `summarize:`, `cola:`) and the output is always text, even if the answer is just `acceptable`. That means one model and one loss can train on every task.

list: **Regression tasks fit too**: STS-B scores a pair of sentences from 1 to 5. The paper finds that the scores are mostly labeled in 0.2 increments, so it rounds each score to the nearest 0.2 and writes it as a string (2.57 becomes “2.6”), turning the task into 21-way classification.

**What if the output isn’t a valid label?** If a classification task produces a word that isn’t one of the labels (the paper’s example is “hamburger”), it is counted as wrong. The paper says their models never did this.
**The exact prefix wording doesn’t matter much**: the paper says changing the wording has limited effect, so it didn’t study it in depth.

blocks.p: The idea isn’t entirely new: earlier work cast all tasks as question answering, and GPT-2 used prompts to get a language model to do tasks zero-shot (see the GPT-2 deep read). T5’s difference is that it allows per-task fine-tuning and handles generation tasks like translation and summarization where the answer space can’t be enumerated.

sections.h: Baseline: an encoder-decoder about the size of BERT-Base

blocks.p: Every comparison starts from the same baseline and changes only one thing at a time, holding everything else fixed. The paper calls this a “coordinate ascent” exploration and admits it may miss interactions between factors.

list: **Architecture**: a standard encoder-decoder Transformer with 12 layers each in the encoder and decoder, sized like BERT-Base at about 220M parameters total. Layer normalization is applied at the input of each sublayer (rescale only, no bias), followed by a residual connection. For position, it uses simplified relative position embeddings: each attention head learns only 32 scalars, bucketed by query-key offset, and all offsets beyond 128 tokens share the same bucket.

**Vocabulary**: SentencePiece is used to split text into 32,000 subword tokens. The tokenizer is trained on a mix of 10 parts English and 1 part each of German, French, and Romanian, to support translation.

**Pretraining**: trained on C4 for 2^{19} = 524,288 steps with batches of about 2^{16} tokens, totaling about 2^{35} (about 34 billion) tokens — roughly one quarter of BERT. The optimizer is Adafactor.
**Fine-tuning**: each task is trained for another 2^{18} = 262,144 steps, and the best checkpoint on the validation set is used.
**Pretraining objective**: randomly mask 15% of tokens; each consecutive masked span is replaced by a single “sentinel” token, and the model only has to output the masked-out pieces.

fig.title: Baseline results, and how much pretraining actually helps
fig.subtitle: From Table 1, validation set. GLUE and SGLUE are average scores across subtasks; CNNDM is ROUGE-2 for summarization; SQuAD is exact match; translation is BLEU.
fig.note: Pretraining brings large gains on every task except English-French translation, where enough training data makes pretraining less helpful. The paper trains the baseline 10 times to estimate run-to-run variance and uses that to judge whether later differences are significant.

callout.title: An experimental habit worth borrowing
callout.text: Many papers report a single run. T5 first trains the baseline 10 times, computes a standard deviation for each metric, and bolds every result within two standard deviations of the best. The paper also warns that small datasets like CoLA, CB, and COPA are extremely noisy — CB’s validation set has only 56 examples — so comparing models by aggregate GLUE or SuperGLUE scores alone requires care.

sections.h: Architecture: encoder-decoder, decoder-only, or prefix language model

blocks.p: Three architectures were popular at the time, differing mainly in attention masking — in other words, who can see whom.

list: **Encoder-decoder**: in the encoder, every position can see the entire input (fully visible). The decoder can see only what it has already generated (causal mask), plus the encoder output through cross-attention. This is the original Transformer and T5 structure.

**Decoder-only language model**: a single Transformer stack concatenates the input and output and uses a causal mask throughout, predicting left to right. The GPT series works this way. The drawback is that even in the input portion each position can see only the tokens to its left, which is worse for reading the input.
**Prefix language model**: also a single stack, but the input part uses fully visible attention and only the output part uses a causal mask. The paper notes that for classification it resembles BERT.

blocks.p: How to compare fairly? The paper notes that parameter count and compute cannot be matched at the same time. An L-layer encoder plus L-layer decoder has about as many parameters as a 2L-layer language model, but only the compute of an L-layer language model: the encoder processes only the input and the decoder only the output, while each layer of a language model processes input plus output.

fig.title: Comparing five architectures
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 (excerpt). P is the parameter count of a 12-layer BERT-Base-sized stack; M is the compute of a 12+12 encoder-decoder.
fig.note: Encoder-decoder with a denoising objective wins on every task. Sharing parameters barely hurts; halving the layers clearly does. The denoising objective always beats left-to-right language modeling.

plain.title: Three rules for who can see what
plain.text: Rows show the position being computed; columns show the positions it can see (dark green = visible). In the encoder of an encoder-decoder, every position can see everything; a language model can see only itself and earlier positions; a prefix language model is a compromise: all prefix positions can see each other, while later positions can still see only earlier ones.

sections.h: Pretraining objective: where to mask, how much, and how

blocks.p: This is the paper’s most detailed section. It demonstrates each objective on the same sentence: “Thank you for inviting me to your party last week.”

fig.title: One sentence, different pretraining objectives: input and output
fig.subtitle: From Table 3. <M> is a shared mask token; <X>, <Y>, <Z> are distinct sentinel tokens; the BERT-style objective also replaces some words with random ones (here, apple).
rows: me to your party last week .
Thank you <M> <M> me to your party apple week .
party me for your to . last fun you inviting week Thank
Thank you <X> me to your party <Y> week .
Thank you me to your party week .
<X> for inviting me <Y> your party last <Z>

plain.title: Cut out a few spans and write only the missing pieces
plain.text: Take a few consecutive spans out of the sentence and replace each hole with a marker (<X>, <Y>). Instead of copying the whole sentence, the model only has to write something like “<X> is for inviting, <Y> is last.” Shorter targets make training much cheaper.

blocks.p: The paper narrows things down in four steps:

list: **Big picture**: BERT-style denoising is best; the prefix language model is close on translation; deshuffling is clearly worst.

**Simplifying BERT**: dropping the random-word replacement step, or only predicting the masked part (replace spans, drop tokens), performs about the same. Predicting only the masked parts makes target sequences much shorter and training faster.
**How much to mask**: they tried 10%, 15%, 25%, and 50%. Differences are small; only 50% clearly hurts GLUE and SQuAD. So they keep BERT’s 15%.

**Masking spans**: instead of masking tokens independently, mask contiguous spans. An average span length of 3 is slightly better than per-token masking on most non-translation tasks, and the sequences are shorter and faster to train.

fig.title: The arithmetic: why predicting only masked spans saves compute
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: a 500-token text with 15% masked. Span-corruption example from Section 3.3.4; other lengths are computed by us from the paper’s rules; the span count for per-token masking is an expectation.
rows: BERT-style: output the full original sentence
fig.note: With span corruption, input = 500 − 75 + 25 sentinels; target = 75 + 25 sentinels + 1 terminal sentinel. Decoder attention cost grows with target length, so shrinking the target from 500 to about 100 makes pretraining far cheaper.

blocks.p: The paper’s summary here is candid: the only clear difference is that denoising beats language modeling and deshuffling. The denoising variants are close enough that **compute cost should drive the choice**. It adds that fine-tuning these objectives further probably has limited upside; the field would gain more from exploring entirely different ways to use unlabeled data.

quiz.q: Which pretraining objective did T5 ultimately use?
options: Predict the next word left to right
Mask 15% of tokens as contiguous spans with mean length 3, replace each span with a sentinel, and output only the masked spans.
Shuffle the sentence and reconstruct it
quiz.why: Span corruption performs about the same as other denoising variants, but has the shortest targets and trains fastest. The paper’s principle: when quality is comparable, choose by compute cost.

sections.h: Data: C4, and why “clean” and “in-domain” matter

blocks.p: C4 starts from Common Crawl’s April 2019 web text. Common Crawl produces about 20TB of text every month, but much of it is menus, error messages, and duplicated content. The paper cleans it with a set of simple rules:

list: Keep only lines ending in a period, question mark, exclamation mark, or closing quotation mark.
Discard pages with fewer than 3 sentences; keep only lines with at least 5 words.
Remove any page containing a word from the “List of Dirty, Naughty, Obscene or Otherwise Bad Words.”
Remove lines containing “Javascript”; remove pages containing “lorem ipsum” placeholder text; remove pages containing curly brackets, since they are mostly code.
Remove Wikipedia-style citation markers and boilerplate policy or cookie notices.
Deduplicate any three-sentence span that appears more than once; use language detection to keep only pages classified as English with probability at least 0.99.

fig.title: What happens if you pretrain on different data?
fig.subtitle: From Table 8 (excerpt), validation set.
fig.note: Uncleaned C4 is worst on every task. In-domain data sometimes helps: Wikipedia + books scores higher on SuperGLUE, almost entirely because of MultiRC, whose data largely comes from fiction.

blocks.p: **In-domain data helps, but it shrinks the corpus.** WebText-like data performs well, but it takes 12x the raw pages to end up with about 1/40 as much data as C4. Smaller data means more repetition — and what does that cost?

fig.title: Too much data repetition hurts
fig.subtitle: From Table 9 (excerpt). Total training is fixed at 2^{35} tokens, using only the first N tokens of C4, so the data is repeated many times.
fig.note: Repeating data 64 times makes little difference, but hundreds or thousands of repetitions clearly hurt. Training loss also drops sharply with smaller data, which the paper takes as a sign the model is memorizing. The recommendation: use the largest dataset you can.

sections.h: Training strategy: how many parameters to fine-tune, and whether to multitask

blocks.p: **Can you get away with fine-tuning only some parameters?** The paper compares two parameter-saving approaches: inserting small “adapter” layers after each feed-forward network and training only those, or “unfreezing” the model layer by layer from the top. Neither beats fine-tuning all parameters. The adapter pattern is that small tasks need only a small inner dimension, while large tasks like translation need a larger one.

fig.title: Partial fine-tuning always underperforms full fine-tuning
fig.subtitle: From Table 10 (excerpt). d is the adapter’s inner dimension
fig.note: The d = 2048 row is identical to the d = 128 row: all seven metrics in Table 10 match exactly (only five are shown here), likely a copy-paste error in the paper. See “Details worth noting” later.

blocks.p: **Multitask training.** In the text-to-text framework, multitask training simply means sampling from a mixture of datasets. The hard part is deciding how much to sample from each task. Sampling proportionally by dataset size lets big tasks crowd out small ones, so the paper sets a cap K per dataset and samples proportionally to that capped size, or uses a “temperature” to flatten the ratios. The result: direct multitask training is worse than “pretraining + separate fine-tuning,” but **pretraining on the multitask mixture and then fine-tuning each task separately** matches the baseline.

fig.title: Multitask training variants
fig.subtitle: From Table 12 (excerpt), validation set
fig.note: “Leave-one-out” means deliberately excluding one task from pretraining and then fine-tuning on it, to simulate seeing a new task. It is only slightly worse, suggesting multitask pretraining does not seriously hurt new tasks. Pretraining on supervised data only, without unlabeled data, is clearly worse on everything except translation.

sections.h: Scale: how to spend 4x more compute

blocks.p: The paper asks a practical question: “If you suddenly had 4x more compute, how would you spend it?” It compares training longer, using larger batches, making the model bigger, and ensembling multiple models.

fig.title: The same 4x compute budget, spent four different ways
fig.subtitle: From Table 13 (excerpt), validation set
fig.note: All of these help. Making the model bigger usually beats simply training longer; a 2x model trained for 2x steps performs about the same as a 4x model, so the two approaches can complement each other. Ensembling works best on summarization and translation but barely helps on SuperGLUE.

blocks.p: The paper also notes the other side of these choices: larger models make downstream fine-tuning and inference more expensive, while extra pretraining of a smaller model can be amortized across many downstream tasks.

sections.h: Putting it together: T5's final recipe and results

blocks.p: The final T5 combines the earlier findings: span corruption (mean span length 3, 15% of tokens masked); pretraining for 1,000,000 steps with batches of 2^{11} sequences of length 512, totaling about 1 trillion tokens — about 32x the baseline; pretraining on a multitask mixture first, then fine-tuning each task separately; and beam search with width 4 for translation and summarization. The model comes in five sizes:

fig.title: Five T5 sizes and their scores
fig.subtitle: From Section 3.7 and Table 14 (excerpt), test set (SQuAD on validation). “Prior best” is as of October 24, 2019.
fig.note: SuperGLUE rises from 84.6 to 88.9, approaching the human score of 89.8. None of the translation tasks beat the prior best; the paper attributes this partly to pretraining only on English, while the best translation systems used data augmentation such as back-translation.

list: **GLUE**: average 90.3, clearly ahead of the prior best on reasoning tasks such as MNLI, RTE, and WNLI.

**SuperGLUE**: a big lead overall, but on two reading comprehension tasks it “exceeds human performance,” which the paper says suggests the metrics may favor machine output. On COPA and WSC, humans score 100%, and the model is still far behind.

**SQuAD**: beats the prior best by more than a point, but it is already above the estimated human level (exact match 82.30), so the paper doubts that continuing to push this leaderboard is very meaningful.
**Summarization**: reaches state of the art, but only ROUGE-2 leads clearly; the paper also notes that a higher ROUGE score does not mean a summary is more coherent.

blocks.p: **How much do the improvements beyond scale matter?** The paper runs one final experiment: it also trains the baseline on 1 trillion tokens (same scale) and compares it with T5-Base, which adds span corruption, multitask pretraining, and other improvements. T5-Base wins on every task, showing that success is not just a matter of scale.

list: **Table 10 has a duplicated row**: the adapter dimension d = 2048 results are identical to d = 128 — all seven metrics match exactly. Since the text says large tasks need larger adapter dimensions, d = 2048 should be better on translation, so this row was likely copied by mistake.

**“Exponential decay” is not actually exponential**: Section 3.1.2 says the learning rate follows 1 / √max(n, k), “held at 0.01 for the first 10^{4} steps, then decaying exponentially.” But 1 / √n is a power-law decay, much slower than exponential decay: by this formula it is about 0.0032 at step 100,000 and about 0.0014 at step 524,288.
**“3B” is actually about 2.8B**: the body text says the 3B variant has about 2.8 billion parameters, but the note in Table 14 says 3 billion.

**The tokenizer description is a bit muddled**: the paper says it “uses SentencePiece to encode text into WordPiece tokens,” while citing the BPE paper and Kudo’s subword regularization paper. These three are related but distinct methods (see the BPE subword tokenization deep read).

**The conclusions carry caveats**: “encoder-decoder is best” holds under pretraining followed by per-task fine-tuning. All comparisons were done at baseline scale while changing one factor at a time, and the paper itself admits they may miss interactions between factors.
**Text-to-text became the default mental model**: today’s large models almost all work through a “text in, text out” interface, and prompting is a natural extension of T5’s task prefixes.
**C4 became a standard pretraining corpus**: C4 makes up 15% of LLaMA’s pretraining data.

**Another ending to the architecture debate**: T5 concluded that encoder-decoder was best, but later large language models (GPT-3, LLaMA, and others) mostly chose decoder-only. One reason is that the goal changed: when models no longer fine-tune per task and instead use prompts to perform tasks directly, a single left-to-right stack is simpler and easier to scale.

**A continuation through multitask and instruction tuning**: T5 found that “multitask pretraining + fine-tuning” was no worse than plain pretraining. Later work such as FLAN trained on many tasks written as natural-language instructions, enabling zero-shot performance on unseen tasks (see this site’s “Alignment and Safety” route).

blocks.p: The next paper in this reading path is **sparse mixture of experts (MoE)**: proposed in 2017 by T5’s second author, Noam Shazeer, it lets a model have a huge number of parameters while using only a small fraction of them at a time.

sections.h: Quiz: did you really get it?

quiz.q: In the text-to-text framework, how is a regression task like STS-B, which requires a score from 1 to 5, handled?
options: Swap in a regression output head
Round the score to the nearest 0.2 and write it as a string for the model to output, turning it into 21-way classification
quiz.why: This is both the cost and the cleverness of “everything is text”: numbers become text too. At test time, if the model outputs a string that is a number between 1 and 5, it is converted back to a float; otherwise it is counted as wrong.

quiz.q: Why does the paper say the pretraining objective “should mainly be chosen by compute cost”?
options: Because the denoising objectives perform about the same, but their target sequences differ greatly in length, and shorter targets train faster
Because the language model objective is best
Because the BERT objective is too complicated
quiz.why: Apart from “denoising beats language modeling and deshuffling,” differences among the other variants are all near the noise floor. Span corruption only outputs the masked parts, shrinking the target length from 500 to about 100.

quiz.q: In the “4x more compute” experiment, which option usually works best?
options: Make the model bigger (2x model for 2x steps, or 4x model), which usually beats only training longer
quiz.why: Making the model bigger usually helps more than only training longer; a 2x model for 2x steps is about the same as a 4x model. Ensembling is strong on some tasks but almost useless on SuperGLUE.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is the text-to-text framework? How are classification, regression, and translation turned into text?
What are the differences among encoder-decoder, decoder-only, and prefix language models? Why can’t parameter count and compute be matched at the same time?
What is T5’s span-corruption objective, and why is it cheaper than the BERT-style objective?
How was C4 cleaned? What effects do cleaning, domain match, and repetition have?
What were the results for partial fine-tuning and multitask training?
With 4x more compute, how does the paper suggest spending it?
What are the shortcomings of T5’s final results?
